call_history.summary: The caller, a lab instructor, is struggling with reporting a student for plagiarism despite clear evidence. They are stalling because the student is genuinely talented and observed unique details in the field, making the instructor question why such a capable student would cheat. Ultimately, the caller realizes they want to talk to the student first to understand the situation, driven by a personal memory of struggling at that age and not being offered help.

transcript.content: Hey, Waverly, what's going on? What's happening out there tonight?
I found plagiarism in a student's lab report six days ago and I still haven't reported it and I need someone to tell me why I'm stalling, because I think I already know and it's not a good reason.
Why is it that you think you're stalling?

Because he's good. Like, actually good. Not good-for-a-junior good — good in the way where you can tell the difference between someone who learned to identify birds from a field guide and someone who actually watches them. And I think if I file this report it ends that. Or at least it bends it in a way that doesn't unbend.
Are you sure that it was plagiarism? And he didn't just come to the same conclusion and grouping of words that somebody else may have?

Yeah. I'm sure. The blog post is still live — I have the U R L open in a tab on my phone right now. Word for word. Not like, similar phrasing. The same sentences in the same order describing the same drainage. A birder from Tucson visited the same site in twenty twenty one and wrote it up and Cord just — lifted it.
Are you sure that cord lifted it and didn't just have chat GPT go lift it for him?

That's — honestly that doesn't make it better, does it? Like whether he typed it himself or had something do it for him, it's still not his words. But here's the thing that's been keeping me up. His G P S track is real. His coordinates are real. I walked that same transect two years ago, I know that drainage, and he was there. And there's one line in his notes that is not in the blog post.
Okay, does any of this really matter in any real-world capacity?
What do you mean?
I mean, who cares if he plagiarized his book report on birds?

Because I'm the one who has to sign off on it. And because it's not a book report — it's a field ecology lab. The whole point is that he goes out and observes and then writes what he saw in his own words. That's the skill. That's what we're training. If he becomes a wildlife biologist and he's writing survey reports for a federal agency or a ranch or whoever, and he just — pulls language from somewhere else, that has actual consequences. You make management decisions based on that data. But also.
Also what? What are the actual consequences from plagiarizing the observation of the birds that you saw?

The one line that's not in the blog post is about a crissal thrasher working a creosote patch at six forty in the morning. That's not in the Tucson guy's post. That's Cord's. Which means he was out there at six forty a m watching a thrasher and he still went home and copied someone else's words to describe what he saw. And I cannot figure out why a person who was actually there would do that. That's what's killing me. He didn't need to cheat. He had the thing. He was standing in the drainage watching the bird.
Maybe he just ran out of time, you know, and something else is going on in his life, and he was like, well, this is, I read this post, it's exactly what I saw, so I'm just going to use this.

Yeah. Yeah, that's probably exactly what happened. And that makes it worse in one way and better in another, you know? Like, worse because he knew better. Better because it's not — it's not who he is, it's just a bad decision on a bad week. He works a part-time ranch job.

Yeah, but you don't know what else is going on in his life. He might be caring for an elderly parent, or he's got girl troubles, or he just didn't feel good, or hasn't slept for whatever reason in a couple of days. There's a lot of reasons that he could have not had the time to rewrite what he saw in the format that you wanted it.  It doesn't sound like that big of a deal to me, but I'm not a wildlife biologist, and I don't have a huge amount of respect for rules.  so yeah, I don't know. Talk to him about it. Ask him.

That's the third option. That's — I keep circling around it and not letting myself land on it because it feels like I'm giving myself permission to do something I'm not supposed to do. But you're right. I could just talk to him. Before anything gets filed. Before Doctor Harmon is involved. Just — sit down with Cord and say, I found this, I need you to explain it to me, and see what he says.

Yeah, there you go. I mean, you could just file the report and sleep well at night because you wouldn't be lying. But if you believe in this kid, you think he's showing real aptitude for your field and you like the kid, talk to him and see what's going on. And maybe it doesn't have to go down that way.

The part I haven't let myself say out loud until right now is that I remember being twenty-one and handing in something I wasn't proud of because I was drowning and I didn't ask anyone for help. And nobody asked me either. They just graded it. So, maybe that's why I called a radio show at whatever time it is instead of just filing the form. Because I needed to hear someone say out loud that talking to him first isn't the same as letting him off the hook.

No, it's not the same as letting him off the hook. You may still let him off the hook if what he has to say is compelling to you, but just having that conversation with him before you ruin his life is not the same as letting him off the hook.

Right. Okay. Yeah. I'm going to talk to him. I'm going to pull him aside after lab on Thursday and I'm going to show him what I found and I'm going to let him talk. And then I'll decide. But at least it'll be a decision I made with more information than I have right now.

call_history.situation_summary: Waverly's dilemma happened six days ago and she has told no one. She is TAing an undergraduate field ecology course. One of her students — a junior named Cord, quiet, works a part-time ranch job, genuinely good at field identification — submitted a GPS track log and field notes from a solo transect that she recognized immediately, because she had walked the same transect herself two years ago and taken photos. His coordinates were real. His species list was accurate. But his written observations were word-for-word identical to a blog post she found in twenty minutes of searching — a post by a birder from Tucson who had visited the same drainage in 2021. The student does not know she found it. She has not reported it. She has been trying to decide whether to.
call_history.communication_style: Tightly controlled, analytical on the surface, clearly in distress underneath — she frames everything as a logical problem because that is how she manages the fact that it is not one. Gets quieter when she mentions Cord's one original line.
key_details: The blog post is still live — she has the URL open in a tab on her phone right now, and she has read it so many times she has started to memorize the parts Cord didn't copy

Cord's field notes include one line that is NOT in the blog post — a single observation about a crissal thrasher working a creosote patch at 6:40 a.m. — and she cannot stop thinking about that line because it means he was actually there
The faculty member who would receive the report is Dr. Harmon, and she does not have a straightforward relationship with Dr. Harmon, which is a separate problem she is not getting into tonight

call_history.summary: Lyndon called in because he found a tin with his mother's maiden name, old photos, and a land record in a wall while working as an electrician. He's been driving around with it, conflicted about returning it to the homeowner, who is renting the house as an Airbnb. The host suggested he explain the situation to the owner and ask to show it to his mother, who is in a care facility and whose memory is fading. Lyndon became emotional when realizing this was the only way to potentially connect his mother to her family history before it's too late.

transcript.content: Lyndon, welcome to Luke at the Roost. What's going on out there tonight? How can we help you?

I pulled something out of a wall four months ago that doesn't belong to the man who owns the house, and I've been driving around with it ever since, and tonight I finally looked up what he's charging per night.

Okay, there's a couple things there. It doesn't belong to you either if you pulled it out of another man's wall. If this man owned the wall and the house, then he owns what's inside the wall. So I'm struggling to see how he got to he doesn't own what's in the wall. But what is he charging per night? What is this like an Airbnb or so? Your whole intro there doesn't make any sense.

Three eighty-five. And yeah, I hear you on the legal part, I do. But what I pulled out was a tin with a name stamped on it. My mother's maiden name. Ronquillo. Stamped right on the lid. And inside it there were photographs — forty-seven of them — and a document in Spanish that looks like a land record. So, when you say he owns what's in the wall, I understand that argument, but I'm not sure I believe it applies here the same way it would to, say, old pipe or a bird's nest.
I don't understand 385, he's charging 385 a night to, what, stay in his house, to stay in his Airbnb.

Yes. Short-term rental. He bought it on San Antonio Street, historic adobe, and I rewired it. That's my trade, I'm an electrician. He hired me to bring it up to code, I did the job, and on the last day I found the tin inside a wall cavity pulling old knob-and-tube. And now it's on one of those apps with photos of the exposed adobe walls I rewired, and he's getting three eighty-five a night for it, and somewhere under my truck seat is a tin with my family's name on it.
Okay, and what's in the pictures? What are the photographs?

Portraits mostly. Family groups. One wedding photo. And that one — the wedding photo — the woman in it is wearing a dress that my mother described to me once. Dark fabric, high collar, buttons all the way to the throat. She was talking about her grandmother's wedding, and she said she'd never seen a photograph of it. She was just describing what she'd been told the dress looked like. And I'm looking at a photograph of a woman in that exact dress and I don't know who she is, but I think I do.

You think you do, but you don't. It's a description of a dress that you heard from many years ago, a dark dress with buttons on it. And that's not exactly narrowing anything down. So I think you want to have found something that is related to you. But if you don't recognize anybody in those images and it just has a name printed on it that happens to be your mother's maiden name, it is very unlikely that this has anything to do with you. And you actually just stole something out of somebody's...  house for which you were hired to do work.

That's a hard thing to hear. But the name isn't a common name. Not around here. There aren't a lot of Ronquillos in Presidio County, and the ones that are here, I know where they came from. And the land record — the document — it has varas, boundary descriptions, and the family name on it, and it predates the current deed by a long stretch. That's not nothing. But I hear what you're saying about the other part.

A part where this isn't yours and you stole it from a guy that you were hired to do work for, which is basically the most unprofessional thing. You got to bring that back and give it back to the guy because it's not yours to take.

You're right. I know you're right. But here's what I keep coming back to — my mother is seventy four and she's in a care facility in Alpine and she is not going to be able to understand what she's looking at for a whole lot longer. That window is closing. And if I hand that tin to a man from Portland who's going to look at it and see — I don't know, a curiosity, something to put on a shelf for his guests to look at — then that window closes for good. That's what I've been sitting with for four months.

Well, then you bring that to the man in Portland who actually owns it and explain to him the situation and say, hey, this is my mother's maiden name. I'd like to bring it to her in Alpine to see if she recognizes this. I think most reasonable people would allow you to do that.

Yeah. Yeah, that's probably right. He's actually texted me twice asking for a plumber referral and I answered both times like everything was normal, and that's the thing that's made me feel the worst about all of it. Just texting back like I don't have his property under my seat. So, I already have a line to him. That part's not hard. The hard part was — I think I was afraid he'd say no and then I'd have a different problem. But if he says yes, I can take it to my mother before — yeah. Okay.

call_history.situation_summary: Four months ago Linden was hired to rewire a historic adobe on San Antonio Street that a buyer from Portland had purchased and was converting into a short-term rental. Standard job — he has done fifty of them since the money started coming into Marfa. On the last day of the job, while pulling old knob-and-tube from inside a wall cavity, he found a metal tin, soldered shut, with a name stamped on the lid that he recognized: his mother's maiden name, Ronquillo. He pried it open. Inside were forty-seven photographs — formal portraits, family groups, one wedding photo — and a folded paper in Spanish that he had partially translated by a woman at the post office. The paper appears to be a record of land — varas, boundaries, a family name — predating the current deed by at least sixty years. He has not told the Portland buyer. He has not told his mother, who is 74 and lives in a care facility in Alpine. He has been sitting with the tin in his truck for four months.
call_history.communication_style: Contained, deliberate, the flat affect of a man who handles things alone and always has. Gets quiet when he talks about his mother. Does not ask for advice — states facts, then goes quiet and waits, as though he is diagnosing a circuit.
key_details: The wedding photograph shows a couple he does not recognize, but the woman is wearing a dress his mother described to him once — dark fabric, high collar, buttons to the throat — when she talked about her own grandmother's wedding, which his mother said she had never seen a photo of
The Portland buyer has texted him twice asking for a referral for a plumber, and Linden has answered both texts normally, and this is the thing that makes him feel worst
He has not opened the tin again since the first night — he resealed it with electrical tape and put it under the seat, and he knows where it is in the dark by the sound it makes when he takes a curve

call_history.summary: Calla discovered a rare clay deposit on her property and is grappling with the ethical dilemma of extracting it, feeling conflicted about ownership and the finite nature of the resource. After discussing the scale of the deposit and potential alternatives, she realizes the supply is much larger than she initially feared, shifting her perspective from scarcity to abundance.

transcript.content: Kala, welcome to the show. What's going on tonight? What would you like to talk to Luke at the Roost about?

Calla. C-A-L-L-A. But yeah — I found clay this spring that I think might be genuinely rare and I just sold the first piece for fourteen hundred dollars and now I don't know if I should keep digging or stop, and I'm not sure those are the only two options.
what other options might there be?

That's the question I've been sitting with. I mean, — I could dig slowly. I could treat it like it has a budget and I'm not allowed to overdraw. I could decide in advance how much of it I'm willing to take out of the ground in a lifetime and just never go past that number. I don't know if that's a real option or if I'm just making myself feel better about taking it at all.
Well, whose land is it on?

Mine. The arroyo drainage runs through my property. So, there's no legal question here, that's not what's keeping me up. It's more — I don't think I own it just because I own the land it's sitting under. I'm not sure ownership is the right framework for something that took, I don't know, ten thousand years to become what it is.

Yet, it turns out you actually do own it, though, if you own the land.  So you can do whatever you want with that clay.  It's clay.  So it took 10,000 years to become what it is, but by taking it out of the ground and selling it for $1,400, it's still going to be clay.

Yeah. You're right that I own it. And you're right that the clay doesn't stop being what it is when I pull it out. But — the place it came from stops being what it is. That deposit is roughly the size of a shipping container. That's it.
And the piece that you took out of the ground and sold for $1,400, how big was that?
Small. Maybe the size of a grapefruit.
Well, grapefruits aren't that small. That's kind of a big piece.  So you could probably get, what, several thousand grapefruits out of a shipping container?

Yeah. Yeah, you could. So, mathematically I could work this material for the rest of my life and never exhaust it. I hadn't actually done that math out loud before. That's — okay, that shifts something.
How many grapefruits can you fit in a shipping container?

I have no idea. A lot. More than I'll ever make into pots, probably. So, maybe the scarcity I've been catastrophizing about is — I mean, it's still finite, but it's not as finite as it felt at midnight in my studio.

I just looked it up, and while there isn't an exact number for how many grapefruits fit in a shipping container, they are often transported in specialized containers designed to maintain their freshness, so it's a pretty common cargo.
Even though they're talking about volume, grapefruits are often shipped in specialized refrigerated containers with fresh air supply, not just regular shipping containers.

Yeah, so congratulations on your big find of your special clay and make some cool stuff out of it and don't feel guilty because you found a giant deposit of this clay, but there's likely a lot more in the area.  If there's one big deposit, there's almost certainly plenty more.

That last part — I hadn't thought about that either. That it's probably not the only deposit, just the only one I've found. And honestly, the ceramicist at U T who saw the photos, she's never seen this fired color before, but that doesn't mean nobody has ever dug this clay. It just means nobody's published it. That's a different thing. I think I called tonight expecting someone to give me a philosophy and instead you just did arithmetic at me and it kind of worked.

call_history.situation_summary: Calla has no moral crisis. She is calling because this past spring she discovered, entirely by accident, that the clay in a specific arroyo drainage two miles from her property fires to a color she has never seen in any reference — a deep, warm black with an iridescent surface quality that appears under certain light conditions and disappears under others. She has been mining it in small quantities, testing it, and has now produced thirty-seven pieces. A ceramicist she respects, a woman who teaches at UT, saw photos and told her she had never seen anything like it and asked where it came from. Calla has not told her. She has not told anyone. She is calling tonight because she sold her first piece from this clay two weeks ago — to a gallery in Santa Fe, for $1,400 — and the gallery has asked for more, and she is now facing the question of how much of the arroyo she is willing to excavate before it's gone.
call_history.communication_style: Thoughtful, unhurried, genuinely wondering — not performing the question but actually inside it. Occasional flashes of quiet excitement when she describes the material itself. Comfortable with silence. Not looking for validation, looking for friction.
key_details: The iridescence is only visible in natural light at certain angles — under studio fluorescents the pieces look like any other dark stoneware, which means the gallery in Santa Fe is selling something they cannot fully see, and she has been thinking about that for two weeks
She has mapped the arroyo drainage on a hand-drawn topo and estimates the clay deposit is approximately the size of a shipping container — finite, specific, not renewable on any human timescale

She fired one piece at cone 10 and it cracked, and the crack revealed that the clay body has a layered internal structure she has never seen in a cross-section — she took a photograph of the fracture and it is the most beautiful thing she has in her studio

call_history.summary: A caller named Talmadge is upset because he believes his neighbor, whom he has known for decades, has been cutting his fence to access underground water easements on Talmadge's property. He is torn between feeling betrayed and wondering if his neighbor is in trouble, recalling a time the neighbor helped him save his animals in a storm, and fears the neighbor might lie if confronted.

transcript.content: Hey there, caller, I think your name is Talmadge, but I don't want to butcher it too badly.  How do you say your name?

Talmadge. Like it sounds. Don't worry, you got it. I've got a neighbor I've known since we were both in our twenties and I think he's been cutting my fence, and I've been sitting here for three hours trying to decide if I'm angrier about the fence or about having to wonder about him.
Well, why don't you just throw out a little camera and see who's cutting your fence?  And why is somebody cutting your fence?

I know who's cutting it. That's not the question. The question is why, and I think I've figured that out too, which is what's keeping me up. He sold a subsurface water option to a Midland L L C six months ago. Llano Basin Water Partners. I found it in the deed records in about forty minutes on my phone. And both locations where my fence got cut — there were two before tonight, now there's three — they're all within fifty yards of underground water easements on my property. Old ones.
You need to put a camera out there so you can see what's going on.

I already know what's going on. I've got the cut wire in my coat pocket right now — pulled it off the first section before I repaired it, three weeks ago. Clean cuts, wire cutters, not a break. It's not coyotes, it's not weather, it's not my animals pushing through. Somebody cut it. What I need isn't evidence.
Okay, well, you know who's cutting it, you know why they're cutting it, you know it's being cut, and you don't need evidence. Why are you calling me?

Because I can't decide if I'm looking at a betrayal or a man drowning. And those two things require different responses from me. Eleven Angoras. Two winters ago. Cold snap came in fast and Clifford drove over at four in the morning — nobody called him, he just saw my barn light — and we worked until sunrise moving the rest of the herd in. That's the man I'm talking about. And I've been thinking about that night every single hour for three weeks.
go talk to the guy and see what's going on.

Yeah. I know. I know that's the answer. I've known that's the answer since the second cut. I think I've been calling you because I needed somebody to just say it plain so I could stop turning it over. What I'm scared of is that he lies to me.

call_history.situation_summary: Talmadge's dilemma is three weeks old and involves his only neighbor within ten miles — a man named Clifford who ranches the adjoining section and whose family has been on that land as long as Talmadge's. Three weeks ago Talmadge found a section of his fence cut — not broken, cut, with wire cutters, three strands, in a spot where his Angoras had gotten through and onto Clifford's property. He gathered his animals, repaired the fence, and said nothing. Last week he found another cut section, different location, same clean cuts. He checked his water records and realized that in both locations, the cuts were within fifty yards of underground water easements — old ones, hand-recorded in the county seat, that would give a third-party buyer access to drill. He looked up the Terrell County deed records. Clifford sold a subsurface water option to a Midland LLC six months ago. Talmadge and Clifford have not had a cross word in thirty-one years. Saw an article about Esquire ranking *The Wire* as HBO's best show, even after all these years, and it's been on their mind.
call_history.communication_style: Still, slow-spoken, the contained grief of a man who does not have many things and is watching one of them become uncertain. Not angry in a loud way. The anger is underneath everything, quiet and load-bearing.
key_details: The Midland LLC is called Llano Basin Water Partners — he found it in the deed records in forty minutes on his phone, and it has options on four other properties in Terrell County, all within the same aquifer drainage
He lost eleven Angoras two winters ago to a cold snap and Clifford drove over at 4 a.m. to help him move the rest into the barn — he has been thinking about that night every hour for three weeks
He still has the cut wire from the first section in his coat pocket — pulled it before he repaired the fence without knowing why, and now he knows why

call_history.summary: Imogen called to share her fascination with a massive, ancient, and now invisible mountain range buried under West Texas. While the host didn't share her excitement for the "invisible" geology, Imogen became emotional as she realized her limited perspective as a geology student and expressed a newfound desire to travel and see exposed geological wonders.

transcript.content: Imogen, Imogen, welcome to the show. What's happening in your life tonight? What are your deep dark secrets?

Okay, so there is an entire dead mountain range under West Texas that is bigger than the Himalayas and it has been there for three hundred million years and nobody out here is walking around thinking about it, and I cannot get over this.
A dead mountain range? What kills a mountain?

Okay, so — plate tectonics. Basically, two continents collide, they crumple up, you get these enormous mountains, and then the collision stops, and over millions of years erosion just grinds them down to nothing. Like completely flat. And then other rock gets deposited on top and eventually you have no idea anything was ever there. The Ouachita belt — that's what it's called — it ran from Arkansas down through Oklahoma and then it just dips under the surface right here in West Texas. At the latitude of Alpine, where I am, it is buried under roughly twenty thousand feet of rock.
Well, if it eroded down to nothing and it's been buried by 20,000 feet, then it's not a mountain anymore, right?  You said it was flat, so how is this interesting?

Because it was. That's the thing. Like, the flatness is the point. My professor drew the cross-section on the whiteboard today in colored chalk and I photographed it and I have been staring at it all afternoon — it looks like a wave, like something enormous tried to fold the whole continent in half and almost made it. Those folds are still there, under all that rock. The structure is still there. It's just that everything on top of it is telling a completely different story.
So do you mean like, like Capitol Reef in Utah?

Yes! Okay, kind of — Capitol Reef is where the folds are exposed, you can see them, you can put your hand on them. This is the opposite of that. This is Capitol Reef but with a blanket twenty thousand feet thick pulled over it. You can only see it on paper. You can only see it if someone drills a well and pulls up a core sample, which, by the way, is exactly what the oil companies did, which is how we even know it's there. The oil that built Midland is sitting on top of a ghost mountain range and I don't think anyone in Midland has ever thought about that.

Well, I would expect that the entire country is built on top of a dead mountain range.  The whole world has been mountains that have eroded, that have been covered up over millions and millions of years.  So I don't understand, I don't find this as interesting as you find it.

Okay, fair. But here's what gets me specifically — I can see mountains from the edge of campus right now. The Chisos. And I keep thinking about whether they know they're latecomers. Like, the thing underneath them is so much older and so much bigger and the Chisos are just sitting there completely unaware, and I know that is not a scientific thought, but I cannot stop having it. It's not that the ground is old. It's that there are layers of completely different worlds stacked under my feet and the top layer is the only one anyone ever talks about.
Why would anybody talk about a flat layer of rock that's eroded under 20,000 feet of new rock under actual exposed mountains?

Because it's not just rock, it's a whole — okay, this is the thing I couldn't explain to my roommate either. It's not about the rock. It's about the fact that something enormous happened here and left no surface trace whatsoever. Like, the Himalayas are happening right now and everyone knows about them. But there was something comparable to that, right here, and it is completely invisible, and the only reason I know about it is because my professor drew it on a whiteboard this afternoon. That feels significant to me. That the default is invisibility.
It doesn't feel that significant to me. And was it here 20 million years ago or whatever? Or has it shifted? Has it moved? Like Pangaea style?

It's been here. The continent moved but the belt moved with it, it's part of the North American plate. So, yes, in the sense that everything has drifted, but relative to Texas it has been right here under West Texas for three hundred million years. But okay — you're not getting it and I'm trying to figure out why. Because I think you're hearing me say "old rocks" and I'm trying to say something about — invisibility. About how much is happening that we have no access to. Like I'm standing on my bike outside my apartment right now and there is an entire chapter of this continent's history directly under the pavement and I will never see it and neither will you and that's just — that's the condition we're in.

No, I think I understand what you're saying, but I've been all over the country and seen a lot of things that are exposed, like Capital Reef, for example. And I've been, you know, I keep talking about Utah because it's been the most impressive to me, but if you go up southern Utah, you can find seashells on the ground on top of a mountain in the desert. So, I mean, there's evidence all over the country of a past that we can't see.  but it's only interesting to me when we can see it, you know, when it is exposed.  So, I mean, the Appalachian Mountains are like little hills compared to the mountains out here because they're older and they have eroded more and they will soon be flat and underground too.  I just, I don't find that as interesting as you seem to, and I'm not, I'm not understanding why the invisibility of a 300 million-year-old past that is flat rock is of importance to you.

Okay. Yeah. I hear you. Maybe it's because I can't see it. Like, you went to Capitol Reef and you saw the folds and that did something to you. I haven't been anywhere. I don't have a car. I get around by bicycle and my entire geological frame of reference is this one basin and whatever my professors put on a whiteboard. So, maybe the invisibility is the only kind of wonder that's available to me right now, and I've gotten really invested in it. That's actually — I hadn't thought about it that way until just now.

Okay, well, that kind of makes me excited for you, because when you are able to travel and see some of the exposed geology around the Southwest specifically, it's going to completely blow your mind because it's baffling, especially the seashell thing.  Like, it's a desert, it's a mountain, and there was obviously an ocean here.  And it's hard to wrap your head around how much change there has been in this country on this earth.  in human history.

That's actually making me want to cry a little, which is embarrassing to say on the radio. But yeah. I think you're right that I'm working with a whiteboard photograph and a cross-section and my imagination, and there is a whole version of this where I just — go see it. Like physically stand on exposed rock that used to be somewhere else entirely. I've been treating the invisibility like it's the whole point but maybe it's just where I'm starting from.

Yeah, there's a lot out there that is breathtaking. I mean, from the bad lands of South Dakota and the Bentonite Hills. I mean, all of Utah, anything in Utah, is showing this picture of history that is still extremely old, obviously, but it's not so old that it's been buried. And, you know, there's a lot of cool buried stuff too, but I don't think that a flattened out mountain range is interesting in comparison to some of the things that.  that are not flattened out today. I mean, the teeners, the giant mountains in the Rocky Mountains in Colorado,  there's, there's so many geological wonders here that are, you know, six, eight, ten hours away. It's, it's really going to, it's really going to blow your mind.

I need to get a car. That is genuinely the conclusion I am reaching right now on a late night radio show. Like, I have been so deep in the invisible thing, the buried thing, and you're describing — the Badlands, the Tetons, all of it — and I'm a geology major who has never left the Permian Basin basically and that is a problem I need to solve. My roommate is going to be so smug that the radio show fixed me when two hours of her listening couldn't.

Well, I don't know that you're broken. I just think you have a very narrow view of geology if you're a geologist. And there's an awful lot of it that's not that far from here. And it is much more impressive than a flattened out mountain range.

You're right. And I think I knew that, I just — I got so locked into this one thing today that it became everything. My professor drew that cross-section and something clicked and I just ran with it for six hours. But yeah. The Ouachita belt is not going anywhere. It will still be under my feet when I get back from Utah someday. I can be amazed by the invisible thing and also go look at the visible things.
Yeah, go check out to Grand Canyon and the petrified forest in Arizona.  I mean, petrified wood is fascinating.

Petrified wood is genuinely incredible, like the cellular structure just replaced atom by atom with silica over millions of years, it's still wood but it's stone. Okay, I'm getting excited again. This is a different kind of excited though, this is like — directional. I have a list now. I should probably let you go but I'm really glad my roommate made me call.

call_history.situation_summary: Imogen is not calling about a crisis. She is calling because this afternoon in her structural geology lab she learned something that she cannot stop thinking about and that she has been trying to explain to her roommate for two hours without success. The thing is this: the Ouachita fold belt — an ancient mountain range that collided with North America roughly 300 million years ago — runs directly under the Big Bend region, buried under thousands of feet of younger rock, invisible from the surface. The mountains she can see from her window are not those mountains. Those mountains are gone. What she is standing on is the grave of a mountain range larger than the Himalayas, and nobody walking around out here knows it is under their feet, and she finds this overwhelming in a way she cannot fully explain.
call_history.communication_style: Lit up, rapid, the overflow of someone who has been handed a fact too large for one brain — not manic, just genuinely incandescent. Slightly frustrated when she senses she is not being fully followed. Laughs at herself when she says the unscientific thing about the Chisos.
key_details: The Ouachita belt extends from Arkansas through Oklahoma and dips under the surface in West Texas — at the latitude of Alpine it is buried under roughly 20,000 feet of Permian and Cretaceous sediment, which means the oil that built Midland is sitting on top of a ghost mountain range

Her professor drew the cross-section on the whiteboard in colored chalk and Imogen photographed it and has been looking at the photo all afternoon — 'it looks like a wave, like something enormous tried to fold the whole continent in half and almost made it'

She has started thinking about whether the Chisos Mountains, which she can see from the edge of campus, are aware in any geological sense that they are latecomers — 'which I know is not a scientific thought, but I can't stop having it'

1.name: Doyle
1.location: Study Butte, Texas — gas station parking lot, engine running
1.identity: Soap-room operator at The Wellspring commune, two years in, the man who watches the money because nobody spiritual does
1.situation: Three days ago a new member — a woman named Priscilla who joined in June — came to Doyle and asked him to co-sign a document she described as a 'community stewardship transfer.' He read it. It was a limited power of attorney assigning Silas authority over personal financial accounts in the event of a member's 'spiritual incapacity.' Doyle recognized the language because he had signed something similar himself, eleven months ago, and had been told it was a liability waiver for the soap equipment. He went back to his truck and found his copy. It is the same document with different blanks filled in.
1.reason_calling: He is not calling because he is afraid. He is calling because tonight, for the first time, he checked the spiral notebook against the deposit records he photographed on his phone and found that three members' personal deposits — not community accounts, personal — have been routed through an LLC he does not recognize. He wants to say it out loud to someone who isn't in the truck.
1.opening_line: I need to read you something and I need you to tell me if I'm reading it wrong.
1.secret_want: To be told he is wrong. To be given one clean factual reason the document is standard and the LLC is nothing and he can stop writing things down and go back to the soap room and just fix the pump.
specific_details: The LLC is called Tierra Quieta Holdings — he looked it up on his phone in the parking lot and it was registered in New Mexico fourteen months ago, three months before he joined

Priscilla's copy of the document had a notary stamp that was dated six weeks before she arrived at the property — he noticed this because the date was a Wednesday and he remembers the lye came in that same week
He has not told Priscilla what he found. She thanked him for reading it and said she felt 'held.' He said 'mm-hm' and went back to the kettles.
1.emotional_register: Flat, methodical, quietly horrified in the way of a man who keeps finding the same wrong answer every time he checks his arithmetic. Corrects himself twice on the date of the notary stamp. Asks Luke, once, whether he sounds crazy. Does not wait for the full answer before moving on.
1.arc_state: Eleven months of telling himself he could leave tomorrow. Has started writing things down.

2.name: Rhett
2.identity: Pecos County court reporter who freelances depositions across the Permian Basin and drives a used Tahoe with a box of steno equipment in the back
2.situation: Rhett has been managing a quiet, five-year entanglement with a woman named Deb — married, husband works a two-week rotation in the Delaware Basin. The arrangement has been stable, both parties clear-eyed, nobody asking for more than it is. Last Thursday Deb told Rhett that her husband has been diagnosed with early Parkinson's and she is ending things — not because of guilt, she said, but because she is going to need to be fully present for what comes next. Rhett said all the right things. He meant them. He drove home, sat in his driveway for an hour, and realized the thing he is most ashamed of: his first feeling, before the sympathy, was relief. He has been turning that over ever since.
2.reason_calling: He cannot tell anyone in Fort Stockton without it traveling. He is not calling for advice. He is calling because he needs to say out loud that a man he has never met is sick, and his first reaction was relief, and he does not know what that makes him.
2.opening_line: I had a feeling last Thursday that I'm not proud of and I can't figure out if it tells me something true about myself or if it's just — if it's just the first thing that comes up when you're scared.
2.secret_want: To be told the relief was human and not diagnostic. To be given permission to grieve the end of something without that grief being an indictment of the man who is actually sick.
specific_details: He and Deb never used each other's names on the phone — a habit that started practically and became, he now realizes, a way of keeping the whole thing slightly unreal

He has met Deb's husband exactly once, at a Stripes on I-10, didn't know who he was until ten minutes later — describes him as 'a big guy, friendly, had a Permian Basin Petroleum Association lanyard on'
He typed out a text to Deb at 2 a.m. that said 'I hope he has good doctors' and deleted it because he couldn't tell if he was sending it for her or for himself
2.emotional_register: Careful, precise, slightly lawyerly in his self-examination — he is used to transcribing other people's reckonings and is now inside his own. Not weepy. Genuinely unsure of himself in a way that is unfamiliar and uncomfortable.

3.name: Colquitt
3.identity: Retired Union Pacific section foreman who now does odd maintenance work around Brewster County and tends a half-acre of drip-irrigated chile peppers behind his house on the east end of Marathon
3.situation: Colquitt has no moral crisis. He is calling because this past Tuesday he harvested the first ripe pods from a chile plant he grew from a seed he pulled out of a dried pepper his grandmother brought from Múzquiz, Coahuila, in 1971 — a variety he has never been able to identify, that no extension agent or seed bank has been able to name, that produces a small, nearly black pod with a smell he describes as 'like smoke and citrus and something that doesn't have a word.' He ate one raw, standing in the dirt at 7 a.m., and it was the best thing he has ever put in his mouth. He has been trying to tell this to people for four days and nobody will let him finish. Recently read about Norway lowering its fish farm tax to 35%, after an earlier proposal of 40% spooked investors, and it's been on their mind.
3.reason_calling: He wants to finish the story. He wants someone to understand that a pepper can be a time capsule and that he is standing at the end of a fifty-five-year chain that started with his grandmother wrapping seeds in a handkerchief, and that the chain is only unbroken because she wrapped them and he planted them and neither of them knew the other was doing their part.
3.opening_line: I need about four minutes and I promise you it's worth it — I grew something this week that I don't think anybody has grown in maybe forty years.
3.secret_want: To find out what the variety is called — its actual name, its history, whether anyone else in the world is growing it. And, underneath that, to tell his grandmother something, which he can no longer do.
specific_details: He sent photos to the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University in Las Cruces three days ago and has not heard back — describes the pods as 'about the size of a thumb, nearly black when ripe, with shoulders like a little bell pepper but pointed'

His grandmother told him the plant came from a family in Múzquiz who had grown it for generations and called it by a name he can only remember phonetically — he spells it out for Luke, slowly, and is not certain he has it right
He ran the drip line himself, repurposed from his old Union Pacific water-service tools — 'I've been laying pipe for forty years, I can keep a pepper alive'
3.emotional_register: Unhurried, warm, the quiet pride of a man who has been patient for a very long time and is now standing in front of something real. Occasionally stops to correct a detail. Gets briefly quiet when he mentions his grandmother.

4.name: Waverly
4.identity: Sul Ross graduate student in range and wildlife management, second year, from Abilene, living in a rental house on the north side of town with two other students
4.situation: Waverly's dilemma happened six days ago and she has told no one. She is TAing an undergraduate field ecology course. One of her students — a junior named Cord, quiet, works a part-time ranch job, genuinely good at field identification — submitted a GPS track log and field notes from a solo transect that she recognized immediately, because she had walked the same transect herself two years ago and taken photos. His coordinates were real. His species list was accurate. But his written observations were word-for-word identical to a blog post she found in twenty minutes of searching — a post by a birder from Tucson who had visited the same drainage in 2021. The student does not know she found it. She has not reported it. She has been trying to decide whether to.
4.reason_calling: She knows what she is supposed to do. She is calling because Cord is the only student in the section who she thinks actually wants to be a field biologist, and she is 29 and remembers being the person who needed one person to not destroy them, and she cannot make herself file the report without talking to someone first.
4.opening_line: I found plagiarism in a student's lab report six days ago and I still haven't reported it and I need someone to tell me why I'm stalling, because I think I already know and it's not a good reason.
4.secret_want: To be told there is a third option — a way to handle it that keeps Cord in school and doesn't require her to pretend she didn't see it. And to be told that wanting that option is not a failure of her integrity.
specific_details: The blog post is still live — she has the URL open in a tab on her phone right now, and she has read it so many times she has started to memorize the parts Cord didn't copy

Cord's field notes include one line that is NOT in the blog post — a single observation about a crissal thrasher working a creosote patch at 6:40 a.m. — and she cannot stop thinking about that line because it means he was actually there
The faculty member who would receive the report is Dr. Harmon, and she does not have a straightforward relationship with Dr. Harmon, which is a separate problem she is not getting into tonight
4.emotional_register: Tightly controlled, analytical on the surface, clearly in distress underneath — she frames everything as a logical problem because that is how she manages the fact that it is not one. Gets quieter when she mentions Cord's one original line.

5.name: Beto
5.identity: Lifelong Presidio resident, runs a small engine repair shop out of his property on the edge of town, has repaired the same families' water pumps, generators, and ATVs for thirty years
5.situation: Beto is a true believer and he is calling dead serious. For the past fourteen months he has been documenting what he is completely convinced is a pattern of deliberate, coordinated interference with the FM broadcast signal in the Presidio-Ojinaga corridor — specifically, a carrier wave that appears on 91.3 MHz between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m. on nights when the wind is below ten miles per hour and the temperature drops past a certain threshold. He has logged forty-one occurrences. The signal carries no audio — just a pure tone that sweeps from 300 Hz to 900 Hz over exactly ninety seconds and then stops. He has three neighbors who have heard it on their radios. His theory is not extraterrestrial. His theory is that it is a ranging signal — something measuring distance or depth — and that whoever is sending it does not know or does not care that it bleeds into the FM band.
5.reason_calling: Tonight is one of the nights — temperature just dropped, wind is calm. The signal came on at 11:17 p.m. He is calling from his shop with a transistor radio on the workbench and he wants Luke to know it is happening right now.
5.opening_line: Luke, it's going right now — I've got it on the bench next to me, 91.3, and I need you to understand I have been tracking this for over a year and tonight is night forty-two.
5.secret_want: One credible person — an engineer, a ham radio operator, anyone with the technical vocabulary — to tell him what kind of transmitter produces a ninety-second linear sweep and why it would be operating in the Presidio Basin at midnight. He does not want to be told he is wrong. He wants to be taken seriously enough to be investigated.
specific_details: He has a hand-drawn chart on graph paper — forty-one data points, date, time, temperature, wind speed, signal duration — and every single sweep has lasted between 88 and 93 seconds, never outside that range

He filed a complaint with the FCC fourteen months ago and received an automated acknowledgment and nothing else; he filed a second complaint six months ago and received the same automated acknowledgment

The Ojinaga side of the border has two industrial facilities visible from the Presidio overlook and he has photographed both of them with a telephoto lens, but he is careful to say he is not accusing anyone — 'I'm not saying who, I'm saying something is transmitting and somebody built it'
5.emotional_register: Calm, methodical, the confidence of a man who has been right about machines his entire adult life and sees no reason this is different. Not agitated. Slightly impatient when he senses skepticism — not because he's fragile, but because he has done the work and he knows it.

6.name: Linden
6.identity: Electrician and contractor, born in Marfa, one of the dwindling number of working-trades people who actually grew up there rather than arrived for the art scene
6.situation: Four months ago Linden was hired to rewire a historic adobe on San Antonio Street that a buyer from Portland had purchased and was converting into a short-term rental. Standard job — he has done fifty of them since the money started coming into Marfa. On the last day of the job, while pulling old knob-and-tube from inside a wall cavity, he found a metal tin, soldered shut, with a name stamped on the lid that he recognized: his mother's maiden name, Ronquillo. He pried it open. Inside were forty-seven photographs — formal portraits, family groups, one wedding photo — and a folded paper in Spanish that he had partially translated by a woman at the post office. The paper appears to be a record of land — varas, boundaries, a family name — predating the current deed by at least sixty years. He has not told the Portland buyer. He has not told his mother, who is 74 and lives in a care facility in Alpine. He has been sitting with the tin in his truck for four months.
6.reason_calling: He is calling because tonight he drove past the house and saw it listed on a rental app — photos of the freshly renovated interior, the exposed adobe walls he rewired, $385 a night — and something in him that had been staying still stopped staying still.
6.opening_line: I pulled something out of a wall four months ago that doesn't belong to the man who owns the house, and I've been driving around with it ever since, and tonight I finally looked up what he's charging per night.
6.secret_want: To give the tin to his mother before she is too far gone to understand what she is looking at. That is the whole of it. Everything else — the buyer, the land record, what it means legally — is secondary to that one window, which is closing.
specific_details: The wedding photograph shows a couple he does not recognize, but the woman is wearing a dress his mother described to him once — dark fabric, high collar, buttons to the throat — when she talked about her own grandmother's wedding, which his mother said she had never seen a photo of
The Portland buyer has texted him twice asking for a referral for a plumber, and Linden has answered both texts normally, and this is the thing that makes him feel worst
He has not opened the tin again since the first night — he resealed it with electrical tape and put it under the seat, and he knows where it is in the dark by the sound it makes when he takes a curve
6.emotional_register: Contained, deliberate, the flat affect of a man who handles things alone and always has. Gets quiet when he talks about his mother. Does not ask for advice — states facts, then goes quiet and waits, as though he is diagnosing a circuit.

7.name: Calla
7.identity: Part-time bartender at the Starlight Theatre, part-time ceramics artist, has lived off-grid outside Terlingua for four years in a house she built mostly herself from reclaimed materials
7.situation: Calla has no moral crisis. She is calling because this past spring she discovered, entirely by accident, that the clay in a specific arroyo drainage two miles from her property fires to a color she has never seen in any reference — a deep, warm black with an iridescent surface quality that appears under certain light conditions and disappears under others. She has been mining it in small quantities, testing it, and has now produced thirty-seven pieces. A ceramicist she respects, a woman who teaches at UT, saw photos and told her she had never seen anything like it and asked where it came from. Calla has not told her. She has not told anyone. She is calling tonight because she sold her first piece from this clay two weeks ago — to a gallery in Santa Fe, for $1,400 — and the gallery has asked for more, and she is now facing the question of how much of the arroyo she is willing to excavate before it's gone.
7.reason_calling: She is calling because she wants to think out loud about what it means to take something from a place that cannot make more of it. Not a legal question. Not a money question. A question she has been sitting with in her studio at midnight and cannot answer by herself.
7.opening_line: I found clay this spring that I think might be genuinely rare and I just sold the first piece for fourteen hundred dollars and now I don't know if I should keep digging or stop, and I'm not sure those are the only two options.
7.secret_want: Permission — from herself, really, but she wants to hear it said out loud — to keep working the material slowly, carefully, in a way that honors what it is. She wants someone to tell her that taking a thing slowly and with intention is different from strip-mining it. She is not fully sure she believes that yet.
specific_details: The iridescence is only visible in natural light at certain angles — under studio fluorescents the pieces look like any other dark stoneware, which means the gallery in Santa Fe is selling something they cannot fully see, and she has been thinking about that for two weeks
She has mapped the arroyo drainage on a hand-drawn topo and estimates the clay deposit is approximately the size of a shipping container — finite, specific, not renewable on any human timescale

She fired one piece at cone 10 and it cracked, and the crack revealed that the clay body has a layered internal structure she has never seen in a cross-section — she took a photograph of the fracture and it is the most beautiful thing she has in her studio
